text: And that’s really the most important part! The reports of the death of building in public are greatly exaggerated. There's no getting around the fact that agentic AI is good at operating in all modalities required to make a video game. I’m sure you’ve seen some of those posts: people are using AI to generate an entire game, based on a few reference images and specifying the mechanics in text. For example, @Stefan_3D_AI 's World of Warcraft clone. Here's another example by @JacobEisner4 : this time of Minecraft. The prompt (provided in the replies) is very concise. You can pick these apart as slop (in many cases they are), but this is the worst these models will be at this behavior, and we should be careful not to move the slopposits as they crush benchmark after benchmark. Models simply didn't have this capability even six months ago; we should all be able to admit that. Recently, I've seen numerous accounts urging people to block an individual, @AdamHoltererer . His crime: instructing state-of-the-art AI models to clone interesting-looking demos of indie games, and posting the videos online. Adam states that he is doing this to benchmark new models like Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. His detractors say he is guilty of theft. I'm not going to get into the ethics of Adam's posts (I think there is a tendency to overreact to him, but he is capable of defending himself), however I will acknowledge I fully understand why indie developers and gamers are taking offense to this. Devs spend a long time refining games to the point where they’re ready to show them on X; and here comes some 18-year-old, purportedly copying their work with a single AI prompt. It’s a scary world to live in! Again, this is the worst these models will ever be at copying games . Just a couple days ago, another user, @WeaselPit , recently claimed he received an from a blackmailer. The person claimed to have fully cloned his game unless he coughed up $200. What this alleged malicious actor is doing would be illegal, and it would quickly be taken down. But with a few texture changes, it's not unreasonable to there is some way you could pull this off legally, leading many to believe you should stop “building in public.” Keep your game secret or else some vibecoder will steal your concept and beat you to the Steam release. But even if this is possible, how likely is it to happen? Let me emphasize that the demos on X display a real capability, but what they measure is narrower than the alarmists would have you think. The model is cloning what it sees . Basic movement, visual style, some obvious mechanics. This is a surface level, shallow clone . Cloning an entire game means the entire system. The writing, the environment, the lore. The sound and the music. Solving game- or immersion-breaking edge cases. In short, how the game feels to play . Not to mention, in order for someone to steal your game, they would have to QA it, market it, build community hype, post it somewhere, and provide post-launch support... the list goes on (as devs are painfully aware). Take a step back and think about the cool demos you've seen on X, especially the ones being cloned, and think about the effort it would really require to productionize it. Even the original devs struggle with that; and he's the one who had all the context that brought the original demo! Making a game is hard and requires artistic effort, and a bit of "magic" to be appealing to players. The "slop thief" who comes across your game will have only ever have a subset of the "magic" of your game. Some will see this argument and say, "how do you explain what happened with 'Needle in a Haystack?'" Does this prove slop theft is already happening (albeit on a micro scale), and we can expect this to scale up to more games? In case you aren't aware of this incident, a creator demoed his game on X and some people saw their opportunity to take his game idea and put out their own pages to capitalize off the hype. Now, there are several clones of this game on Steam and it's hard to tell who the original creator was. Kind of like finding a... well, you know. This is kind of analogous to the mockbuster phenomenon. Low-budget studios would hear about the upcoming release of the next big Pixar movie, and capitalize off of the existing marketing (in this case, organic viral marketing). They then release a movie with similar-looking characters and art (often before the real movie!), in the hopes of duping little Timmy's grandma as she roots through the Walmart bargain bin before the new movie comes out. Now, I'm not saying a videogame "slopbuster" strategy would be completely ineffective, but my point is Ratatouille (released June 27th , 2007) wasn't ultimately overshadowed by the mockbuster Ratatoing (released June 26th , 2007), so neither will the original Needle-In-Haystack game. Additionally, "Needle In A Haystack" is not exactly on the level of a Pixar movie. There is really not a whole lot of complexity to the idea or execution, so there is fundamentally less to clone, meaning it's more likely you could steal this concept successfully. Most people are not making a game this simple (although, perhaps they should ). So, you might tighten the claim and say, "well, maybe large games are safe, but small games are vulnerable!" Well, then this example is self-refuting. Even this game, the prototypical example of "AI cloning is real," has 23,000 playtesters alone. None of the "slop clones" come even remotely close. One wonders if these slopbuster devs would have better luck just producing their own viral hit! I’ve made the case that AI cloning games makes little financial sense, and is unlikely to go beyond those “benchmark” tech demos you see on X. Even knowing that, why does it still make us feel uncomfortable? This may be discomfort about AI, generally, dressed up as discomfort for stealing games, specifically. The fact is, we live in a world where you can create something in one prompt that use to take hundreds of hours just a couple years ago. Sure, we've been tending that direction for some time (I re-made Tetris for a pre-college assignment in 2016), but this is a quantum leap. Things are changing so fast, and it's easy to despair. There's too much to address than this one article can get into, but I'll say this: My firmly-held belief that human art intrinsically has value is why I think AI has great potential to help indie devs. It's easier than ever for an artistic, but less technically skilled, game dev to get in the game and tell their story, and that seems like a good thing to me. Just like YouTube helped people like Kane Parsons and Curry Barker hone their skills and to release high-quality art, AI will help the next generation of human artists get their foot in the door. So, keep honing your craft. And don't be afraid to show it to the world!
